title: Why Fabric Craft Matters: Issey Miyake and the Person Behind Him
excerpt: We aren't discussing fabric because they are “Issey Miyake.” They became “Issey Miyake” because they cared about fabric.
body:
We aren't discussing fabric because they are “Issey Miyake.” They became “Issey Miyake” because they cared about fabric.

“First I close my eyes and let the fabric tell me what to do.” That is how Issey Miyake, now 77, [described](http://designhistoryforum.org/dd/papers/vol01/no1/01_1_35_43.pdf) his design process.

Last month he opened a retrospective of his half-century career at the National Art Center, Tokyo. He said little on stage about the past. Instead he brought up a craftsman in Shiroishi, Miyagi Prefecture, who had mailed him a sample of washi paper. He tried making it into a jacket.

[“It doesn't wrinkle at all!”](http://www.theguardian.com/fashion/2016/apr/10/issey-miyake-45-years-at-the-forefront-of-fashion) He was thrilled.

[Makiko Minagawa](http://www.kci.or.jp/research/dresstudy/pdf/D58_MINAGAWA_Interview_Japanese_Textile_ENG.pdf) first met Issey Miyake in 1971, just as the Miyake studio opened. Paris's May 1968 uprising had ended three years earlier; Janis Joplin and Jimi Hendrix, the rock musicians who led the American hippie movement, had died the year before. Minagawa had come to ask his advice about moving to London. It went differently than she expected. She became the textile design director of the Issey Miyake brand, and the two have now worked together for 45 years.

In the five years before they met, Miyake had steeped himself in the West: a year of haute couture at the École de la Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne in Paris, three years as an assistant to Guy Laroche and Givenchy, then, after he reached New York in 1969, a year under the minimalist designer Geoffrey Beene.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171051WxGe3ZQHh9abXoiR.jpg-w600)

![The École de la Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne in Paris, image from the school's website](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171051ytAoVNY1uQalxhHr.jpg-w600)

Those five years left him with two conclusions that would run through his thinking for the rest of his life — conclusions similar to the reasons the West would later, in the 1980s, [file Rei Kawakubo and Yohji Yamamoto under the label “Japan shock.”](https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=Wtkm3O3nWXkC&pg=PA140&lpg=PA140&dq=%22Japan+Shock%22+Issey+Miyake&source=bl&ots=nSgjnR5EQy&sig=hJLKfu0awW3XaSGKZDmxr0ok5AE&hl=zh-CN&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwi2lNmlrcnMAhXKIcAKHR_YAaIQ6AEIKTAB#v=onepage&q=%22Japan%20Shock%22%20Issey%20Miyake&f=false) The first was doubt about the Western way of designing “from the outside in” — drape cloth over a mannequin, then cut, sew and pleat it into an ideal female line. Miyake preferred the kimono's “from the inside out” approach, which starts with the relationship between body and garment and treats cloth as a person's “second skin.” Clothes, in this view, should be **“made from a single piece of cloth” (*One piece of cloth*).**

The second came from the spirit of freedom and equality he felt in the May uprising and the hippie movement, which convinced him that fashion's “Western aesthetic determinism” had to go. Rather than make couture for a small circle of rich people, he wanted to start from ready-to-wear (*prêt-à-porter*) and pursue **“Universal Clothing”** — pieces like T-shirts and jeans that serve people anywhere, at any time.

This is where Miyake's own design language began. But the answer to both problems was the same: **fabric**. Making a garment “from a single piece of cloth” works like making a kimono. Kimono shapes barely vary, so richer effects have to come from the cloth itself — from dyeing, weaving and other techniques. And inside that framework, “Universal Clothing” means a designer has to understand how different cultures think about fabric, and how they make it.

![A variety of shibori patterns, image from oliverands.com](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171052J4p8iGQTLUKIDv9O.jpg-w600)

![Shibori generally uses six dyeing methods](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171052xD2vtKdY3zS8QXlC.jpg-w600)

In 1971, with the studio newly opened in Japan and Miyake's ideas badly in need of physical form, Makiko Minagawa was indeed the right person.

If textiles and clothing mattered to prewar Japan roughly the way semiconductors and cars matter today, by the 1960s ancient crafts like **shibori** (indigo dyeing) had all but died out. The Japanese public wanted Western labels — Missoni, Prada, Gap. [The railway had not even reached](http://www.amazon.com/Memory-Cloth-Yoshiko-Iwamoto-Wada/dp/1568364709) Arimatsu in Aichi or Narumi on Honshu, the birthplaces of shibori.

What made Minagawa rare was her family. Freshly graduated with a degree in textiles, she came from one of the last households in Kyoto still practicing traditional fabric craft: her grandfather hand-dyed silk kimono, her father designed cloth for Japanese folding screens. And like Miyake, she liked to start from traditional fabric and take on hard new problems.

“Working with Miyake is like holding a conversation about Zen. One day he suddenly said, ‘the white of winter.’ That was all. So I started guessing — the white of ice and snow? The white of a salt pond? The white porcelain of Korea's Joseon dynasty? Usually that kind of exchange produces an answer at once, but that time it took me a year, starting with the choice of raw material for the yarn.” It is always like this at the Miyake studio: [two to three years can pass between the first fabric samples and the finished garment](https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=6hCMBfLTPZwC&pg=PA77&lpg=PA77&dq=Minagawa+++Issey+Miyake&source=bl&ots=CulgPvvz3V&sig=kmkRRLTP7WD6hSxsviQsYwUB5Zk&hl=zh-CN&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwjd4s7Lp8fMAhUFKsAKHaiKDnE4ChDoAQgtMAA#v=onepage&q=Minagawa%20%20%20Issey%20Miyake&f=false), with everyone in the studio working on the idea together.

![*Tattoo*, image from the Kyoto Costume Institute, which Issey Miyake helped found](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171053hq1NM2aZflU7ueBc.jpg-w600)

The studio's first fall/winter collection, shown in 1971, made waves in the Western fashion world. Its most discussed piece, [*Tattoo*](http://www.kci.or.jp/archives/digital_archives/detail_195_e.html), was built on fabric Minagawa created: a light-brown knit dress that used traditional Japanese techniques to print Jimi Hendrix and Janis Joplin — the two young American rock musicians who had died in 1970 — across the back, as if saluting the spiritual leaders of the hippie movement. Modern rock crossed with traditional tattoo art, youth culture colliding with tradition: nobody had seen anything like it.

The American textile designer Jack Larsen [observed](http://designhistoryforum.org/dd/papers/vol01/no1/01_1_35_43.pdf) that “Miyake and Minagawa follow Japanese tradition in their fabric techniques and their choice of color, often using shibori, nishiki (brocade weaving) and similar methods, with cool colors and no strong contrasts. But in their choice of materials, their final treatment of sheen and stretch, and their control of production costs, they are thoroughly modern.” They were fusing East and West through the cloth itself.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171053BqgbkIhACzw4ZQna.jpg-w600)

![The 1982 Body Works exhibition. The pieces used no cloth at all — they were made from plastic, paper or wire. A rattan-woven top resembling a Japanese samurai garment ran on the cover of Artforum, the first piece of fashion ever to appear on the cover of an art magazine.](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021710549wRE1JOZxY7Vqf4y.jpg-w600)

![1983, the [Bodyworks photography collection](http://www.worldfoodbooks.com/tag/shozo-tsurumoto/), shozo tsurumoto](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171054wNWklrXB6IiF42YL.jpg-w600)

![Seashell Coat, 1980s](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171055HNE845MmGQOxrJob.jpg-w600)

From 1981, Miyake began to find the Japanese kimono too narrow a starting point. He should reach past Japan to the whole of the East. So he sent designers to Guatemala, Bali, India and Tibet to dig up local techniques and then adapt them for mass production. Minagawa was one of them; she [went to India](http://www.anothermag.com/fashion-beauty/8651/haat-the-fashion-brand-preserving-japanese-artistry?utm_source=Link&utm_medium=Link&utm_campaign=RSSFeed&utm_term=haat-the-fashion-brand-preserving-japanese-artistry) in 1983.

“That trip affected me enormously. I saw the fine skill and delicate handwork of the local craftsmen, and the measures the Indian government had taken to protect handicraft, and it made me think about the situation back in Japan. Japan was developing fast then, industrial mass production was racing ahead, and the whole country was full of roaring factories. That did save me a great deal of trouble, and I enjoyed working with synthetic fibers. But I did not want to forget the appeal of natural materials and natural methods.”

Perhaps that is why, the next year, in 1984, Miyake began arguing for traditional Indian fabric in modern clothing. He set up a sub-brand called “ASHA” and staged two exhibitions of Indian handloom weaving, one in Paris and one in Tokyo.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171056XJk6zd3xQ75ADSCh.jpg-w600)

![Pleats Please as shot by various photographers, images from [*Pleats Please*](http://www.itsnicethat.com/articles/issey-miyake-pleats-please), published by Taschen](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171056kETRLdxHnAc8it7m.jpg-w600)

![The 1993 Pleats Please launch](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171056ZPjgL1cVhJnCTYBM.jpg-w600)

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171057p9deiMtwsWPBrVgO.jpg-w600)

![Work shot by the photographer Irving Penn](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171058Rhm47x8rkBAiQsSG.jpg-w600)

By the 1990s, everything the studio had poured into traditional fabric craft and new technology produced a change in kind. The two dreams of thirty years earlier — “Universal Clothing” and clothes “made from a single piece of cloth” — became real, and became the two most recognizable collections in the Issey Miyake line.

**Pleating** was a technique the studio had worked on since 1988. It appeared in 1993 as the collection “Pleats Please Issey Miyake.” The method cuts the cloth larger than the finished size, then pleats it by machine and sets the pleats with heat, so flat fabric turns three-dimensional — carrying on the Japanese habit of leaving “empty space” between cloth and skin. That gave the clothes structural beauty and give, and it opened a new idea: fabric can define a garment's shape and its function.

Then in 1998, clothes “made from a single piece of cloth” arrived too, through a collaboration with the textile engineer Dai Fujiwara, as the **A-POC (A Piece Of Cloth)** project. Computers ran the whole process, starting from a single thread and finishing the fabric, the texture and the garment in one pass.

![Pleating: the cloth is sandwiched between two sheets of paper and pleated](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171058os0FkMg5Qtj3Abf4.jpg-w600)

![A-POC](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171059OLgHinMkVAy7QPut.jpg-w600)

By 1999, Issey Miyake had stepped back from day-to-day work, and Minagawa, who had always stood behind the scenes, started thinking about a sub-brand of her own — doing the same thing she had always done: finding where traditional fabric craft meets modern production.

Go to Minami-Aoyama in Tokyo's Minato Ward and, among the Issey Miyake brand's six boutiques and 11 sub-brands, you will find Makiko Minagawa's Haat. “Haat” sounds like the English “heart,” means “market” in Hindi, and looks close to the Hindi word “Haath,” hand. [“We can change our techniques and processes cleverly, even use machine weaving, and still carry the warmth of the maker's hand through.”](http://www.anothermag.com/fashion-beauty/8651/haat-the-fashion-brand-preserving-japanese-artistry?utm_source=Link&utm_medium=Link&utm_campaign=RSSFeed&utm_term=haat-the-fashion-brand-preserving-japanese-artistry)

![The Haat store in Tokyo, image from the Issey Miyake website](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171059hw20UxuPjE5HNqcZ.jpg-w600)

Haat has become the Miyake sub-brand that digs deepest into traditional craft. Take the Ultimate Black collection of spring/summer 2014, whose extremely full black came out of an Edo-period dyeing method. “In Japan this black is used only for formal occasions — weddings, funerals. One of our craftsmen told us the technique exists because his grandfather spilled egg white on a black kimono and found that the protein reacted with the dye and made the black blacker. We turned that traditional technique into a new chemical one.”

Another time Minagawa looked at the gray balls of fluff inside a Roomba vacuum cleaner and decided the gray was exactly right. She went to an organic cotton spinning workshop, collected a pile of waste fiber, and asked traditional weavers in Japan's Tohoku region to help turn it into an extraordinarily soft scarf. Those scarves have been part of the HaaT collection since 2011.

Last year, Minagawa's work on fabric made her one of the six Game Changers 2015 in architecture and design named by Metropolis magazine.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171100GMImjbWvFQfAiLDR.jpg-w600)

![Spring/summer 2014, the Ultimate Black collection](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171100IN0vm8BS6ohxwJFr.jpg-w600)

![Fall/winter 2014, inspired by Japanese paper lanterns. The whole fabric was woven on a jacquard loom from a single warp thread, with the weft using different textures for different effects; the white is cotton with cashmere, and the black yarn has a polyester core.](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171101B73HE40UbtTayDWR.jpg-w600)

![Spring/summer 2015, made with a German folk heat-gradient technique](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171102QL7JOcAdVn6ErIYm.jpg-w600)

![Spring/summer 2016,
the black sections and the yellow sections were dyed with two different tie-dye techniques](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021711025ZFuGfBjeP3UaR2i.jpg-w600)

While his old partner was busy with all this, Miyake was not idle either. In 2007, at nearly 70, he founded Reality Lab to study environmentally friendly fabrics, then released the 132.5 collection made of recycled polyester, and the IN-EI Lighting series with the Italian company Artemide.

Looking back, why stay this stubbornly devoted to fabric craft for a whole lifetime? In [Minagawa's words](http://www.whitewallmag.com/design/atelier-visit-makiko-minagawa-from-isse-miyakehaat): “Honestly, handwork has become more expensive, and the difference is only slight. With inkjet the black comes out a little lighter; done by hand in Kyoto it comes out fuller. That is the size of the difference.” She thinks the extravagant step is worth taking, because “I have a responsibility to pass these crafts on.”

[And Miyake?](http://www.nytimes.com/2014/12/02/fashion/issey-miyakes-50-years-of-making-connections.html?_r=0) “What interests me most is still the person, and the human form. Nothing comes closer to a person than cloth.”

![Makiko Minagawa, image from [metropolismag.com](http://www.metropolismag.com/January-2015/Game-Changers-2015-Makiko-Minagawa/)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171103c1ZDR9U2IJgaGd0j.jpg-w600)

![Issey Miyake, image from [the-rosenrot.com](http://the-rosenrot.com/2012/08/the-brilliance-of-issey-miyake-a-retrospective.html)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171103JvMk3pQ7Wc0Ldg8U.jpg-w600)
